```{r setup}
library(treatseqr)
```

# Introduction

This vignette demonstrates backwards transitions in `treatseqr` using a
relapsing and remitting multiple sclerosis (RRMS) setting. In contrast to
oncology treatment-sequence models, where disease progression is typically
assumed irreversible (with some possible exceptions in the future!), RRMS
patients may experience true relapses, reversing the disease progression. 

In modelling terms, this just means that patients can return to earlier
treatment lines, depending on the context. Furthermore, it may also be the case
that some states are progressive (i.e., don't have backwards transitions),
whilst others allow regression (e.g., after a surgical intervention which may
reverse the progression of the disease). This is precisely the
backwards-transition mechanism built into `treatseqr`.

One important caveat to this is that if the *number* of cycles through this
process of going backwards, then this should be structured as a "progressive"
structure, i.e., states further along the pathway even if in reality they are
not. This will allow the `treatseqr` approach to provide you with separate state
residency per cyclical state. For instance, if patients can only get a surgery
once, but the hazard of exiting the relapsed state remains the same, then this
must be structured downstream of the surgery. This is because for those people,
the probability of getting surgery every cycle is 0, and not the transitions
from `tp_source`! Even if using the same transition probabilities, you should
then construct a post surgery relapse state to impose that treatment pathway
construct/rule.

The example in this vignette does the opposite to this. It assumes that **it
doesn't matter how many relapses you have**, you can theoretically infinitely
loop between the surgery and relapse states. The probability of this happening
tends to zero, but it's an important distinction worth noting here. If the
treatment pathway does have a lot of complicated rules like this, the
applicability of `treatseqr` will start to wane as you will need more and more
states to capture the different contexts (and separate sojourn times) that
patients are faced with in reality. The use of a patient-level state transition
probability model becomes much more appealing in this setting, because you can
track the individual history of patients as they are simulated, allowing the
implementation of rules based on sojourn times, or even combinations of sojourn
times that will inevitably be substantially more flexible than a single unified
sparse matrix approach could efficiently capture. That being said, health
economic models in real health technology assessment settings ubiquitously
impose such simplifying assumptions, so this becomes a strategic choice at some
stage in the conceptualisation exercise.

The model represents escalating levels of disease burden as a sequence of tunnel
states. A brief model-entry pre-tunnel state (`newly_dx`) routes patients into
`stage_1` which is itself modelled as a full-length tunnel. Note that this means
that it doesn't matter how *long* a patient was in the newly diagnosed stage,
their subsequent transition probabilities will be the same. To extend this, one
would establish "fast" and "slow" transition probabilities to two *different*
tunnels, thereby capturing `stage_1` given a particular element of patient
history. This spreads the data thinner but demonstrates that an exact solution
is still possible with `treatseqr`. In English, you'd split `stage_1` into
`stage_1_fast` and `stage_1_slow`, and code your model such that patients don't
transition into the fast version after a certain time point. This idea can be
extended substantially with some creativity and careful coding, which is why we
mostly leave the generation of the transition probabilities up to you in this
package.

Going back to this example, modelling `stage_1` as a tunnel (rather than a
pre-tunnel state) is what allows the backwards-transition mechanism to work: in
`treatseqr`, transitions from within a tunnel back to an earlier state can only
target other **tunnel** start positions, so any state that needs to *receive*
backwards transitions must itself be a tunnel state.

The `d` dimension of `stage_1` (see the more basic vignettes for explanation)
tracks how long a patient has been continuously in the between-relapse state
since their last relapse resolution. Patients who resolve from `stage_2` back to
`stage_1` re-enter at `d = 1`, resetting this counter. To go beyond this point
of sophistication in a generalised way essentially requires unlimited
dimensionality to the transition probability matrix. It is possible that this
has no solution in many situations, or that the solution is bespoke to a given
context.

`treatseqr`'s 2-d matrix-based approach can handle simpler settings (like the
above small extension) very well by simply growing larger. However, this could
very easily go out of control if you try to replicate a full complex
microsimulation pathway tracking patient history in a multidimensional way.
Nevertheless, `treatseqr` might be a good place to start during
conceptualisation with dummy transition probabilities so that you can concretely
identify whether you need to move over to patient-level approaches. It will
become very apparent very quickly if you need to track patient history in a more
complex way.

In this example, during each relapse tunnel, patients may:

- Relapse, returning to the start of the previous tunnel at any cycle `d = 1, 2,
…, r_len`, not just at the end.
- Progress, advancing to the next relapse level, again possible at any cycle
during the relapse.
- Die, going directly to the final absorbing state.
- Remain in the relapse. For this one, what happens at the **end of the tunnel**
  starts to become very important. For instance, if `p_stay > 0`, then patients
  accumulate at the end of the tunnel, and if `p_stay = 0` then they are forced
  out of it at the end (i.e., a decision-tree node). See the vignette
`fixed-duration-tunnels` for an example with accumulation and the consequences
of that.

In this example, patients who reach the most severe stage enter a secondary
progressive tunnel with no possibility of reversal. This allows you to capture
those early-line benefits, potentially alleviating some of the Jensen's
inequality ($E[f(x)] \ne f(E[x])$) problems which ultimately push towards
patient simulation in this context. In other words, the benefit of early line
remission could be non-linear as the consequences actually accelerate, which
means that earlier line treatments become more cost-effective overall.

The five model states are:

| State | Type | Tunnel length | Clinical meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `newly_dx` | Pre-tunnel | — | Model entry at RRMS diagnosis |
| `stage_1` | Full-length tunnel | `th` | Minimal disability (EDSS 0-2); between relapses |
| `stage_2` | Fixed-duration (DTN) | `r_len` | Active relapse, moderate disability (EDSS 3-4) |
| `stage_3` | Fixed-duration (DTN) | `r_len` | Active relapse, severe disability (EDSS 5-6) |
| `stage_4` | Full-length tunnel | `th` | Secondary progressive phase (EDSS 7+); irreversible |

# Model specification

```{r specify_m}
r_len <- 3L
th <- 40L

m_spec <- specify_m(
  tunnel_lengths    = c(th, r_len, r_len, th),
  pre_tunnel_states = 1L
)

m_spec$matrix_size
```

The total matrix size is `r m_spec$matrix_size`: 1 pre-tunnel state + `r th` + 3
+ 3 + `r th` tunnel cycles + 1 death state.

# Transition probabilities

Backwards and forward transitions within the relapse tunnels are non-zero at
every `d`, rising toward the decision-tree node at `d = r_len`. Note that
destinations with no transition probability can be given as `NULL`. These will
automatically changed to zeros by the validator, which will then be dropped
before populating the sparse matrix to maximise the computational efficiency of
the extrapolation.

```{r define_tps}
tp_source <- list(
  # ------------------------------------------------------------------
  # newly_dx (pre-tunnel): vectors of length th
  #   nearly all patients enter stage_1 immediately after diagnosis;
  #   small background mortality
  # ------------------------------------------------------------------
  newly_dx = list(
    stage_1 = rep(0.97, th),
    stage_2 = NULL,
    stage_3 = NULL,
    stage_4 = NULL,
    die     = rep(0.01, th)
    # implied p_stay = 0.02 every cycle
  ),

  # ------------------------------------------------------------------
  # stage_1 (full-length, th cycles): minimal disability
  #   low but ongoing relapse risk each cycle
  # ------------------------------------------------------------------
  stage_1 = list(
    stage_2 = rep(0.06, th),
    stage_3 = NULL,
    stage_4 = NULL,
    die     = rep(0.01, th)
    # implied p_stay = 0.93 every cycle
  ),

  # ------------------------------------------------------------------
  # stage_2 (fixed-duration, r_len cycles):
  #   d = 1, 2 : resolution or progression possible but not certain
  #              — p_stay > 0, most patients remain in the relapse
  #   d = 3    : decision-tree node — p_stay = 0, all probability
  #              allocated to resolution, progression, or death
  #
  #   stage_1 (backwards): relapse resolves without disability gain
  #   stage_3 (forward):   relapse progresses to higher disability
  # ------------------------------------------------------------------
  stage_2 = list(
    stage_1 = c(0.15, 0.20, 0.50), # backwards: rises each cycle
    stage_3 = c(0.05, 0.08, 0.40), # forward:   rises each cycle
    stage_4 = NULL,
    die     = c(0.02, 0.02, 0.10)
    # d=1 implied p_stay = 0.78
    # d=2 implied p_stay = 0.70
    # d=3 implied p_stay = 0.00  (decision-tree node)
  ),

  # ------------------------------------------------------------------
  # stage_3 (fixed-duration, r_len cycles):
  #   d = 1, 2 : partial resolution or progression possible
  #   d = 3    : decision-tree node — p_stay = 0
  #
  #   stage_2 (backwards): partial resolution; returns to moderate relapse
  #   stage_4 (forward):   enters secondary progressive phase
  # ------------------------------------------------------------------
  stage_3 = list(
    stage_2 = c(0.10, 0.15, 0.35), # backwards: rises each cycle
    stage_4 = c(0.03, 0.08, 0.50), # forward:   rises each cycle
    die     = c(0.03, 0.03, 0.15)
    # d=1 implied p_stay = 0.84
    # d=2 implied p_stay = 0.74
    # d=3 implied p_stay = 0.00  (decision-tree node)
  ),

  # ------------------------------------------------------------------
  # stage_4 (full-length, th cycles): secondary progressive — no reversal
  #   rising mortality reflects continued disease progression
  # ------------------------------------------------------------------
  stage_4 = list(
    die = seq(0.05, 0.20, length.out = th)
  )
)
```

# Validating transition probabilities

```{r validate}
valid_tp <- validate_tp_source(
  tp_source      = tp_source,
  tunnel_lengths = c(th, r_len, r_len, th)
)

lobstr::tree(
  rapply(valid_tp, function(x) round(x, 3), how = "list")
)
```

The validator expands every state's inner list to cover all destinations. Those
supplied as `NULL` or omitted entirely are filled with zeros. For example,
from `newly_dx`, stages 2-4 are empty as we want to channel patients through the
pathway in order.

# Early resolution and progression within relapse tunnels

Because transition probabilities are non-zero at `d = 1` and `d = 2`, patients
can exit the relapse tunnel before reaching its final cycle. We can inspect the
full probability table at each `d`:

```{r stage2_exit}
# Probabilities out of stage_2 at each tunnel cycle d (rows = destinations):
s2_exit <- do.call(rbind, lapply(valid_tp$stage_2, identity))
rownames(s2_exit) <- names(valid_tp$stage_2)
round(t(s2_exit), 3)
```

```{r stage2_pstay}
# Implied p_stay at each cycle of stage_2:
1 - rowSums(round(t(s2_exit), 3))
```

```{r stage3_exit}
# Probabilities out of stage_3 at each tunnel cycle d:
s3_exit <- do.call(rbind, lapply(valid_tp$stage_3, identity))
rownames(s3_exit) <- names(valid_tp$stage_3)
round(t(s3_exit), 3)
```

```{r stage3_pstay}
# Implied p_stay at each cycle of stage_3:
1 - rowSums(round(t(s3_exit), 3))
```

At `d = 1` and `d = 2` the row sums are less than 1, confirming that most
patients remain in the relapse that cycle. The probabilities rise across `d`,
reflecting increasing clinical pressure to resolve or progress as the relapse
continues. At `d = r_len = 3`, the row sums are exactly 1.

```{r dtn_check}
# Confirm decision-tree node: row sums at d = r_len must equal 1
rowSums(round(t(s2_exit), 3))[r_len]
rowSums(round(t(s3_exit), 3))[r_len]
```

This design allows some nuance. Early exits occur at `d = 1` and `d = 2`, but
the DTN at `d = 3` essentially forces patients into different states. This
simulates something along the line of a response assessment or some clinical
check in point wherein progression would be assessed and patients would be
categorised. Conceptually, this gives you a lot of flexibility as you can
capture these clinical checkpoints, or even impose structural scenarios in your
model where they happen at different time points! We have not experimented with
adding a probabilistic element here such that in the PSA or even the OWSA the
time point that forces a decision tree could be varied, but this should be
possible by carefully writing some functions to build in that flexibility. Note
that if you do something like this, you will then only be able to evaluate the
consolidated trace consistently. The states will still be the same and in the
same order, but the number of sub-states in each state will change (i.e., a
different `m_spec` per PSA iteration!) which could get very confusing! If you do
want to implement something like this, please contact the authors as we will be
interested in use cases and the demand for a feature like this.

# Progressive phase is one-way

`stage_4` is an end-stage severity, essentially best supportive care until
death.

```{r stage4_tps}
round(valid_tp$stage_4$die, 3)
```


# Generating M and extrapolating

As with the other vignettes, use the function to generate our matrix list:

```{r generate_m}
m <- generate_m_list(
  m_specification = m_spec,
  transition_prob_list = valid_tp,
  state_names = c(
    "newly_dx", "stage_1", "stage_2", "stage_3", "stage_4", "die"
  )
)
```

Before extrapolating, it is instructive to visualise `m2` directly. In addition to
the superdiagonal strips (patients advancing along tunnels) and rightward
vertical strips (forward transitions to later tunnels), the relapse blocks
contain leftward vertical strips — the backwards transitions. These are absent
in the purely progressive models presented in the other vignettes.

```{r plot_m2}
m2_df <- as.data.frame(Matrix::summary(m$m2))

# label each entry by source tunnel block
s1_end <- 1L + th
s2_end <- s1_end + r_len
s3_end <- s2_end + r_len
s4_end <- s3_end + th

m2_df$source <- cut(
  m2_df$i,
  breaks = c(0L, s1_end, s2_end, s3_end, s4_end, s4_end + 1L),
  labels = c("stage_1", "stage_2", "stage_3", "stage_4", "death")
)

ggplot2::ggplot(
  m2_df,
  ggplot2::aes(x = j, y = i, colour = source, alpha = x)
) +
  ggplot2::geom_point(size = 2) +
  ggplot2::scale_y_reverse() +
  ggplot2::scale_alpha_continuous(range = c(0.3, 1), name = "Probability") +
  ggplot2::labs(
    title    = "Sparsity pattern of m2",
    subtitle = "Backwards strips appear to the left of each relapse block",
    x        = "Destination (column j)",
    y        = "Source (row i)",
    colour   = "Source state"
  ) +
  ggplot2::theme_minimal()
```

In the `stage_2` block (rows `r th + 2`-`r th + 4`) the leftward strip at column
2 represents resolution back to `stage_1`. In the `stage_3` block (rows
`r th + 5`–`r th + 7`) the leftward strip at column `r th + 2` represents partial
resolution back to `stage_2`. The `stage_1` block has no leftward strip. It is
the first tunnel so there is no earlier tunnel to resolve into.

The `stage_4` block similarly has no backwards strip, reflecting the one-way
nature of secondary progressive disease. Opacity represents
probability.

Finally, we can extrapolate the trace:

```{r extrapolate}
trace <- extrapolate_treatseqr(m = m, spec = m_spec)
```

A quick sanity check — column sums of the trace should equal 1 throughout:

```{r check_trace}
colSums(trace)
```

# Consolidation and outputs

Consolidate the expanded trace to something we're used to seeing in health
economics:

```{r consolidate}
res <- consolidate_treatseqr_trace(
  full_trace  = trace,
  spec        = m_spec,
  state_names = m$state_names
)
```

## State populations over time (`t`)

As with the other vignettes, we can plot the traces:

```{r plot_t}
graphics::matplot(
  res$t,
  type = "l", lty = 1,
  xlab = "Cycle", ylab = "Population",
  main = "State populations over absolute time"
)
graphics::legend(
  "topright",
  legend = colnames(res$t),
  col    = seq_len(ncol(res$t)),
  lty    = 1,
  cex    = 0.8
)
```

Several features of this trace are worth noting:

- `newly_dx` empties out quickly. Almost all patients have entered `stage_1` by
  cycle 2. This is just a function of the probability of exit.
- `stage_1` remains populated throughout the horizon. Because patients can
resolve from `stage_2` back to `stage_1`, this state is continuously replenished
and never fully drains, so it doesn't approach zero as quickly as you might
expect.
- `stage_2` is also sustained longer than in a strictly forward model. The
feedback loop keeps replenishing the moderate-relapse population.
- `stage_4` grows gradually as severe relapses progress to secondary
  progressive disease; from there, the only exit is death.

Note: you can experiment with longer time horizons to see what happens over a
longer time period. To do this, just change `th` right at the start of this
vignette and run through. The trace looks a bit more like "the norm" when you
set it to `200`. The reason it is set to `r th` is so that the plot of `m2` is
clearer!

## Within-tunnel survival (`d`) and the feedback-loop problem

The `d` output captures the population distribution across `d = 1, …` for each
tunnel at each model cycle. In the absence of any re-entries into a tunnel, the
`rowSums` of a tunnel's rows in the full trace matrix would give a clean
within-tunnel survival curve.

In this model, however, patients can re-enter both `stage_1` and `stage_2` via
backwards transitions:

- `stage_2` to `stage_1` feeds patients back to `d = 1` of `stage_1`, mixing
  re-entry patients with patients on their first visit.
- `stage_3` to `stage_2` feeds patients back to `d = 1` of `stage_2`, similarly
  contaminating its `d = 1` slot.

As a result, `res$d` for `stage_1` and `stage_2` accumulates contributions from
multiple cohorts (first-entry and re-entries). However, unlike the case where
patients are held at the end of tunnels, the baseline value in `d = 0` for a
tunnel state is based on total traffic into the state. Consequently, the
`d`-based survival curves are actually valid but are polluted by people
entering the state at different points in wall time (`t`).

However, because of the fundamental "clock-reset" assumption in this package,
`t` has no effect on transitions in a tunnel state, meaning you can use these
as within-state survival curves. Just be aware that the disjoin between `t` and
`d` may have practical implications for mortality probabilities within the
tunnels. The implicit assumption is that the mortality only depends on `d`, and
not `t`, meaning that aging has no effect on them. 

This is another reason to jump to patient-level simulation modelling. If the
model is further complicated by needing to capture some ever-growing `t`-based
*relative* mortality rate, then the limit of our approach is exceeded and
patient simulation is a more appropriate option. For instance, if a standardised
mortality ratio is used to multiply (age and sex-matched) general population
hazard, and this is powering the transition to death, rather than recorded
Kaplan-Meier, the tunnel states do not track wall time. Because wall time is not
relevant to tunnel states, time since baseline is not tracked and therefore age
(and therefore sex) distribution is unknown during tunnels. It then becomes
important to consider how your death probabilities are being derived, and if bias
is being introduced via the general population hazard moving above that being
implemented by the tunnel-state. Only patient-level simulation can handle this
well, as it can be used to tweak exit probabilities every cycle for every person
simulated to respect the data generating process for the death probabilities.

Most of the time, however, in our field the mortality rates are substantially
above those of the general population, and this is not a concern. Nevertheless,
please ensure you plot the implied hazard of overall survival (essentially the
gradient of `1 - dead` in the $t$ based trace) in your model to ensure that it
does not drop below that of the general population!

```{r plot_d}
graphics::matplot(
  res$d,
  type = "l", lty = 1,
  xlab = "Cycles since tunnel entry", ylab = "Proportion remaining",
  main = "Within-tunnel d, case including backwards transitions"
)
graphics::legend(
  "topright",
  legend = colnames(res$d),
  col    = seq_len(ncol(res$d)),
  lty    = 1,
  cex    = 0.8
)
```


## Expected time in state

The total expected cycles spent in each state across the cohort:

```{r expected_time}
round(colSums(res$t), 2)
```
